claim: Polyubiquitin chains linked through all lysines of ubiquitin exist.
source: Although polyubiquitin chains linked through all lysines of ubiquitin exist, specific functions are well-established only for lysine-48 and lysine-63 linkages in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Specific functions are well-established only for lysine-48 and lysine-63 linkages in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Although polyubiquitin chains linked through all lysines of ubiquitin exist, specific functions are well-established only for lysine-48 and lysine-63 linkages in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The K11R mutant had strong genetic interactions with threonine biosynthetic genes.
source: The K11R mutant had strong genetic interactions with threonine biosynthetic genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: K11R mutants import threonine poorly.
source: Consistently, we found that K11R mutants import threonine poorly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The K11R mutant exhibited a strong genetic interaction with a subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC).
source: The K11R mutant also exhibited a strong genetic interaction with a subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC), suggesting a role in cell cycle regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: K11-linkages are important for vertebrate APC function.
source: K11-linkages are important for vertebrate APC function, but this was not previously described in yeast.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: K11-linkages were not previously described in yeast APC function.
source: K11-linkages are important for vertebrate APC function, but this was not previously described in yeast.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The yeast APC modifies substrates with K11-linkages in vitro.
source: We show that the yeast APC also modifies substrates with K11-linkages in vitro, and that those chains contribute to normal APC-substrate turnover in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: K11-linked chains contribute to normal APC-substrate turnover in vivo.
source: We show that the yeast APC also modifies substrates with K11-linkages in vitro, and that those chains contribute to normal APC-substrate turnover in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Ubiquitination regulates the DNA damage response.
source: Ubiquitination regulates a broad range of important cellular pathways including the DNA damage response (Jackson and Durocher, 2013; Harper and Elledge, 2007), apoptosis (Broemer and Meier, 2009), cell cycle progression (Borg and Dixit, 2017), immune and inflammatory responses (Wertz and Dixit, 2010), and transcription (Geng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ubiquitination regulates apoptosis.
source: Ubiquitination regulates a broad range of important cellular pathways including the DNA damage response (Jackson and Durocher, 2013; Harper and Elledge, 2007), apoptosis (Broemer and Meier, 2009), cell cycle progression (Borg and Dixit, 2017), immune and inflammatory responses (Wertz and Dixit, 2010), and transcription (Geng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ubiquitination regulates cell cycle progression.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Three enzyme classes mediate the covalent attachment of ubiquitin to target proteins: E1, E2, and E3.
source: Three enzyme classes mediate the covalent attachment of ubiquitin, a 76 amino acid protein, to target proteins: An E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme activates ubiquitin for transfer to an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, which in turn interacts with an E3 ubiquitin ligase to transfer ubiquitin to lysine residues on the target protein (Hershko and Ciechanover, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ubiquitin is a 76 amino acid protein.
source: Three enzyme classes mediate the covalent attachment of ubiquitin, a 76 amino acid protein, to target proteins: An E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme activates ubiquitin for transfer to an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, which in turn interacts with an E3 ubiquitin ligase to transfer ubiquitin to lysine residues on the target protein (Hershko and Ciechanover, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ubiquitin has seven acceptor lysines (K6, K11, K27, K29, K33, K48, and K63).
source: Ubiquitin has seven acceptor lysines (K6, K11, K27 K29, K33, K48, and K63), all of which are used in vivo to generate polyubiquitin chains (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: All seven lysines of ubiquitin are used in vivo to generate polyubiquitin chains.
source: Ubiquitin has seven acceptor lysines (K6, K11, K27 K29, K33, K48, and K63), all of which are used in vivo to generate polyubiquitin chains (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K48 and K11 are the most abundant ubiquitin linkage types in yeast, each accounting for about a third of ubiquitin linkages.
source: K48 and K11 are the most abundant ubiquitin linkage types—each accounting for about a third of ubiquitin linkages in yeast—while the remaining five are present in relatively lower amounts (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: K6, K27, K29, K33, and K63 linkages are present in relatively lower amounts than K48 and K11 in yeast.
source: K48 and K11 are the most abundant ubiquitin linkage types—each accounting for about a third of ubiquitin linkages in yeast—while the remaining five are present in relatively lower amounts (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: K48-linked chains adopt a closed conformation with ubiquitin's hydrophobic patch being sequestered at the interface between two adjacent ubiquitin protomers.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, adopt a closed conformation with ubiquitin's hydrophobic patch being sequestered at the interface between two adjacent ubiquitin protomers (Komander and Rape, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains assume an extended conformation devoid of non-covalent contacts between ubiquitin monomers.
source: In contrast, K63-linked chains assume an extended conformation devoid of non-covalent contacts between ubiquitin monomers (Datta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K48-linked chains specify proteins for proteasomal degradation.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in the DNA damage response.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in protein trafficking.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in mitophagy.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in inflammation.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in immune responses.
source: K48-linked chains, for example, specify proteins for proteasomal degradation (Chau et al., 1989), while K63-linked chains have non-degradative roles in various signaling pathways including the DNA damage response (Harper and Elledge, 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Ulrich, 2005; Spence et al., 1995; Wang and Elledge, 2007), protein trafficking (Lauwers et al., 2009; MacGurn et al., 2012), mitophagy (Ordureau et al., 2015), inflammation (Deng et al., 2000; Grabbe et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2001), and immune responses (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Degradative functions of K11 linkages in endoplasmic reticulum biology have been described.
source: Degradative functions of K11 linkages in endoplasmic reticulum biology as well as Hedgehog signaling in fruit flies have been described (Xu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013), while the critical role of K11-linkages in mitotic progression in metazoans has been studied in detail (Meyer and Rape, 2014; Williamson et al., 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2008; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Degradative functions of K11 linkages in Hedgehog signaling in fruit flies have been described.
source: Degradative functions of K11 linkages in endoplasmic reticulum biology as well as Hedgehog signaling in fruit flies have been described (Xu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013), while the critical role of K11-linkages in mitotic progression in metazoans has been studied in detail (Meyer and Rape, 2014; Williamson et al., 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2008; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K11-linkages play a critical role in mitotic progression in metazoans.
source: Degradative functions of K11 linkages in endoplasmic reticulum biology as well as Hedgehog signaling in fruit flies have been described (Xu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013), while the critical role of K11-linkages in mitotic progression in metazoans has been studied in detail (Meyer and Rape, 2014; Williamson et al., 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2008; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K6, K27, K29, and K33 ubiquitin linkages are especially rare in cells.
source: Although K6, K27, K29, and K33 ubiquitin linkages are especially rare in cells (Xu et al., 2009; Dammer et al., 2011), important observations have contributed to an increasing recognition of their physiological relevance (Akutsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K6-linked polyubiquitin chains function in the DNA damage response through the BRCA1-BARD1 E3 ligase in a proteolysis-independent manner.
source: K6-linked polyubiquitin chains, for example, are reported to function in the DNA damage response through the BRCA1-BARD1 E3 ligase in a proteolysis-independent manner, as well as in mitophagy, through the E3 ligase, Parkin (Ordureau et al., 2015; Nishikawa et al., 2004; Christensen et al., 2007; Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K6-linked polyubiquitin chains function in mitophagy through the E3 ligase Parkin.
source: K6-linked polyubiquitin chains, for example, are reported to function in the DNA damage response through the BRCA1-BARD1 E3 ligase in a proteolysis-independent manner, as well as in mitophagy, through the E3 ligase, Parkin (Ordureau et al., 2015; Nishikawa et al., 2004; Christensen et al., 2007; Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K27-linkages have been linked to mitophagy, as some Parkin substrates are decorated with K27-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: K27-linkages have also been linked to mitophagy, as some Parkin substrates are reportedly decorated with K27-linked ubiquitin chains (Birsa et al., 2014; Geisler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: mRNA stability is regulated by K29-linked ubiquitin chains on HuR via an interaction with UBXD8.
source: mRNA stability is regulated by K29-linked ubiquitin chains on HuR, an mRNA binding protein, via an interaction with UBXD8, an adaptor for the essential p97 ATPase (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K33-linked ubiquitin chains regulate post-Golgi protein trafficking by mediating the interaction of Coronin-7 with Eps15.
source: Finally, K33-linked ubiquitin chains have been suggested to regulate post-Golgi protein trafficking by mediating the interaction of Coronin-7 with Eps15, a trans-golgi network protein (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A comprehensive examination of the roles of K6, K11, K27, K29, and K33 ubiquitin linkages is lacking, particularly in yeast.
source: Notwithstanding these and other intriguing observations (Silva et al., 2015; Song et al., 2010; Elia et al., 2015), a comprehensive examination of the roles of K6, K11, K27, K29, and K33 ubiquitin linkages is lacking, particularly in yeast.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The lack of comprehensive examination of atypical ubiquitin linkages is owed to partial redundancy of ubiquitin acceptor lysines.
source: This is owed to both the partial redundancy of ubiquitin acceptor lysines (Xu et al., 2009), and the technical limitations of current protein analysis methods (Swatek and Komander, 2016; Carrano and Bennett, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as reasoning supported by citation.

claim: The lack of comprehensive examination of atypical ubiquitin linkages is owed to technical limitations of current protein analysis methods.
source: This is owed to both the partial redundancy of ubiquitin acceptor lysines (Xu et al., 2009), and the technical limitations of current protein analysis methods (Swatek and Komander, 2016; Carrano and Bennett, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as reasoning supported by citation.

claim: Genetic interaction analysis has been a powerful tool for discovering novel gene functions.
source: Genetic interaction analysis, namely the study of the phenotypic effects of combining mutations, has long been a powerful tool for discovering novel gene-functions by revealing functional relationships between genes (Dixon et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2001; Tong et al., 2004; Schuldiner et al., 2005; Braberg et al., 2013; Costanzo et al., 2010; Costanzo et al., 2016; Sarin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The engineered yeast strains express ubiquitin at levels comparable to wild-type yeast.
source: The engineered yeast strains express ubiquitin at levels comparable to wild-type yeast (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lysine 48 of ubiquitin is essential.
source: Because lysine 48 of ubiquitin is essential (Finley et al., 1994), strains expressing K48R ubiquitin also contained 20% wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Strains expressing K48R ubiquitin contained 20% wild-type ubiquitin.
source: Because lysine 48 of ubiquitin is essential (Finley et al., 1994), strains expressing K48R ubiquitin also contained 20% wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Two biological replicates of the ubiquitin SGA had a correlation coefficient of 0.42.
source: Nonetheless, two biological replicates of the ubiquitin SGA had a correlation coefficient of 0.42, in line with other large genetic interaction screens (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ubiquitin SGA is similarly enriched for genetic similarity within physically interacting gene pairs when compared to the chromosome biology E-MAP.
source: Although the genetic profiles of gene deletions in the ubiquitin SGA include only 17 queries (i.e. the lysine mutants), the screen is similarly enriched for genetic similarity within physically interacting gene pairs when compared to the published chromosome biology E-MAP, wherein the genetic interaction profiles contain 754 queries and is biased for genes with known related functions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ubiquitin SGA identified known gene modules based on their genetic interactions with K-to-R ubiquitin mutants.
source: As expected, the ubiquitin SGA identified known gene modules based on their genetic interactions with the K-to-R ubiquitin mutants.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: rim101Δ, rim21Δ, ygr122wΔ, and dfg16Δ form a cluster in the ubiquitin SGA.
source: For example, rim101Δ, rim21Δ, ygr122wΔ, and dfg16Δ form a cluster in the ubiquitin SGA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All four genes rim101, rim21, ygr122w, and dfg16 are members of the Rim101 pathway.
source: All four genes are members of the Rim101 pathway, whose eponymous gene is a transcription factor that is activated in response to alkaline conditions in a manner dependent on Rim21, Ygr122Wp, and Dfg16 (Maeda, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The K11R ubiquitin mutant has relatively few strong genetic interactions.
source: Indeed, the K11R ubiquitin mutant has relatively few strong genetic interactions, suggesting that K11 linkages have a narrow set of functions in yeast (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: K11 linkages have a narrow set of functions in yeast.
source: Indeed, the K11R ubiquitin mutant has relatively few strong genetic interactions, suggesting that K11 linkages have a narrow set of functions in yeast (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that K11R has few strong genetic interactions.

claim: The negative genetic interaction between ubc4Δ and K27R is reproducible and specific.
source: The negative genetic interactions observed between ubc4Δ and K27R and between hom2Δ and K11R proved to be reproducible and specific (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The negative genetic interaction between hom2Δ and K11R is reproducible and specific.
source: The negative genetic interactions observed between ubc4Δ and K27R and between hom2Δ and K11R proved to be reproducible and specific (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of CDC26 in combination with mutation of ubiquitin's K11 or K48 caused significant synthetic growth defects.
source: Deletion of CDC26 in combination with mutation of ubiquitin's K11 or K48 caused significant synthetic growth defects, whereas only a mild negative interaction was observed in cdc26Δ and K33R double mutant cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only a mild negative interaction was observed in cdc26Δ and K33R double mutant cells.
source: Deletion of CDC26 in combination with mutation of ubiquitin's K11 or K48 caused significant synthetic growth defects, whereas only a mild negative interaction was observed in cdc26Δ and K33R double mutant cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gene ontology term enrichment analysis of the K11R mutant genetic interactome revealed a striking enrichment of genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis.
source: Characterization of the K11R mutant genetic interactome using gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis revealed a striking enrichment of genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis (Figure 3A) (Huang et al., 2009a; Huang et al., 2009b), suggesting a possible role of K11 linkages in amino acid homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletions of HOM2 or HOM3 exhibited strong genetic interactions specifically with the K11R ubiquitin mutants.
source: Deletions of HOM2 or HOM3, two genes involved in the biosynthesis of homoserine, a threonine and methionine precursor (Mountain et al., 1991), and to a lesser extent deletion of GLY1, which encodes an enzyme that generates threonine and glycine (Liu et al., 1997), exhibited strong genetic interactions specifically with the K11R ubiquitin mutants (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: HOM2 and HOM3 are involved in the biosynthesis of homoserine, a threonine and methionine precursor.
source: Deletions of HOM2 or HOM3, two genes involved in the biosynthesis of homoserine, a threonine and methionine precursor (Mountain et al., 1991), and to a lesser extent deletion of GLY1, which encodes an enzyme that generates threonine and glycine (Liu et al., 1997), exhibited strong genetic interactions specifically with the K11R ubiquitin mutants (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GLY1 encodes an enzyme that generates threonine and glycine.
source: Deletions of HOM2 or HOM3, two genes involved in the biosynthesis of homoserine, a threonine and methionine precursor (Mountain et al., 1991), and to a lesser extent deletion of GLY1, which encodes an enzyme that generates threonine and glycine (Liu et al., 1997), exhibited strong genetic interactions specifically with the K11R ubiquitin mutants (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The synthetic growth defect in K11R and hom2Δ or hom3Δ double mutant cells is rescued by either homoserine or threonine.
source: Rescue of the synthetic growth defect by either homoserine or threonine suggested that K11-linked polyubiquitin chains function redundantly with threonine biosynthesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: K11-linked polyubiquitin chains function redundantly with threonine biosynthesis.
source: Rescue of the synthetic growth defect by either homoserine or threonine suggested that K11-linked polyubiquitin chains function redundantly with threonine biosynthesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The genetic interactome of the K11R ubiquitin mutant is most similar to deletions of GNP1 and YDR509W.
source: Comparison of a comprehensive yeast genetic interaction network to the genetic interactome of the K11R ubiquitin mutant revealed that it is most similar to deletions of GNP1 (Ryan et al., 2012), a high-affinity threonine permease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Regenberg et al., 1999), and YDR509W, a dubious open-reading frame that overlaps the N-terminus of GNP1 and is thus likely to also abrogate GNP1 expression (Fisk et al., 2006) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GNP1 is a high-affinity threonine permease.
source: Comparison of a comprehensive yeast genetic interaction network to the genetic interactome of the K11R ubiquitin mutant revealed that it is most similar to deletions of GNP1 (Ryan et al., 2012), a high-affinity threonine permease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Regenberg et al., 1999), and YDR509W, a dubious open-reading frame that overlaps the N-terminus of GNP1 and is thus likely to also abrogate GNP1 expression (Fisk et al., 2006) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K11R ubiquitin mutant cells have a significant defect in threonine import.
source: To assess that model, the import of radioactively labeled threonine into wild-type and K11R ubiquitin cells was measured, revealing a significant defect in the K11R ubiquitin mutant, and thus showing that K11 linkages promote threonine import (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by threonine uptake assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: K11 linkages promote threonine import.
source: To assess that model, the import of radioactively labeled threonine into wild-type and K11R ubiquitin cells was measured, revealing a significant defect in the K11R ubiquitin mutant, and thus showing that K11 linkages promote threonine import (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by threonine uptake assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Doa10 is responsible for approximately 50% of K11 linkages in yeast cells.
source: Deletion of DOA10, an endoplasmic-reticulum-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase that is responsible for approximately 50% of K11 linkages in yeast cells (Zattas and Hochstrasser, 2015; Xu et al., 2009), in combination with hom2Δ also led to a synthetic growth defect that was rescued by homoserine (Figure 3G), suggesting that Doa10, along with K11 ubiquitin chains, contribute to threonine import.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Deletion of DOA10 in combination with hom2Δ led to a synthetic growth defect that was rescued by homoserine.
source: Deletion of DOA10, an endoplasmic-reticulum-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase that is responsible for approximately 50% of K11 linkages in yeast cells (Zattas and Hochstrasser, 2015; Xu et al., 2009), in combination with hom2Δ also led to a synthetic growth defect that was rescued by homoserine (Figure 3G), suggesting that Doa10, along with K11 ubiquitin chains, contribute to threonine import.
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Doa10, along with K11 ubiquitin chains, contribute to threonine import.
source: Deletion of DOA10, an endoplasmic-reticulum-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase that is responsible for approximately 50% of K11 linkages in yeast cells (Zattas and Hochstrasser, 2015; Xu et al., 2009), in combination with hom2Δ also led to a synthetic growth defect that was rescued by homoserine (Figure 3G), suggesting that Doa10, along with K11 ubiquitin chains, contribute to threonine import.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The APC is a highly conserved and essential E3 ubiquitin ligase that governs the metaphase to anaphase transition and mitotic exit.
source: The anaphase promoting complex (APC) is a highly conserved and essential E3 ubiquitin ligase that governs the metaphase to anaphase transition and mitotic exit by ubiquitinating several substrates, including securin and S and M-phase cyclins (Sumara et al., 2008; Tyers and Jorgensen, 2000; Thornton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The APC ubiquitinates securin and S and M-phase cyclins.
source: The anaphase promoting complex (APC) is a highly conserved and essential E3 ubiquitin ligase that governs the metaphase to anaphase transition and mitotic exit by ubiquitinating several substrates, including securin and S and M-phase cyclins (Sumara et al., 2008; Tyers and Jorgensen, 2000; Thornton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In yeast, the APC cooperates with two E2 ubiquitin conjugases, Ubc4 and Ubc1.
source: In yeast, the APC cooperates with two E2 ubiquitin conjugases, Ubc4 and Ubc1, to decorate its substrates with polyubiquitin chains and target them for proteasomal degradation (Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ubc4 is a promiscuous E2 that monoubiquitinates or initiates short ubiquitin chains on substrates.
source: Ubc4 is a promiscuous E2 that monoubiquitinates or initiates short ubiquitin chains on substrates (Arnason and Ellison, 1994; Kirkpatrick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ubc1 extends initial modifications with long and homogenous K48-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Ubc1 subsequently extends those initial modifications with long and homogenous K48-linked ubiquitin chains (Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007; Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K48 of ubiquitin is necessary for processive APC-substrate ubiquitination in vitro.
source: K48 of ubiquitin is necessary for processive APC-substrate ubiquitination in vitro (Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007), and is the only linkage type required for normal cell cycle progression in vivo (Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K48 is the only linkage type required for normal cell cycle progression in vivo.
source: K48 of ubiquitin is necessary for processive APC-substrate ubiquitination in vitro (Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007), and is the only linkage type required for normal cell cycle progression in vivo (Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cdc26 aids in the assembly and promotes the stability of the APC holoenzyme at high temperatures.
source: At high temperatures, a non-essential subunit of the APC, Cdc26, aids in the assembly and promotes the stability, of the APC holoenzyme (Schwickart et al., 2004; Zachariae et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K48R ubiquitin mutant cells lacking Cdc26 exhibit a significant growth defect.
source: As expected given the well-established role of K48 linkages in APC-mediated proteasomal degradation, K48R ubiquitin mutant cells lacking Cdc26 exhibit a significant growth defect (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The role of K11-linked polyubiquitin chains in metazoan APC-substrate turnover is well understood.
source: Although K11-linked polyubiquitin chains had not been previously reported to function in APC-substrate degradation in yeast, their role in metazoan APC-substrate turnover is well understood (Meyer and Rape, 2014; Williamson et al., 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2008; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The metazoan APC interacts with two E2 enzymes, Ube2C and Ube2S, that sequentially ubiquitinate substrates.
source: Analogous to the yeast APC, the metazoan APC interacts with two E2 enzymes, Ube2C and Ube2S, that sequentially ubiquitinate substrates (Wu et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ube2c initially modifies substrates with monoubiquitin or short chains that are then elongated by Ube2S with K11-linked chains.
source: Ube2c initially modifies substrates with monoubiquitin or short chains that are then elongated by Ube2S with K11-linked chains (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cell-cycle-regulated levels of securin and several cyclins were altered in K11R ubiquitin mutants relative to cells expressing wild-type ubiquitin.
source: Indeed, cell cycle analysis experiments with cells lacking Cdc26 revealed that the cell-cycle-regulated levels of securin and several cyclins were altered in K11R ubiquitin mutants relative to cells expressing wild-type ubiquitin (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mitotic cyclin Clb2 persisted much longer during mitosis in K11R cells, with its disappearance being delayed by almost 30 min.
source: For example, the mitotic cyclin Clb2 persisted much longer during mitosis in K11R cells, with its disappearance being delayed by almost 30 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The levels of Clb3 and Pds1 were misregulated in K11R mutant cells, although to a lesser extent than Clb2.
source: The levels of the S/M cyclin, Clb3, and of the Separase-inhibitor, Securin (Pds1), were also misregulated in K11R mutant cells, although to a lesser extent than Clb2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Clb5 is normally targeted for degradation during the M and G1 phases by the APC.
source: Clb5, an S-phase cyclin, is normally targeted for degradation during the M and G1 phases by the APC (Ostapenko et al., 2015; Shirayama et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The expression of Clb5 during both M and G1 was elevated in K11R mutant cells.
source: Its expression during both M and G1 was elevated in K11R mutant cells, suggesting that K11 was required for complete turnover of this substrate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: K11 is required for complete turnover of Clb5.
source: Its expression during both M and G1 was elevated in K11R mutant cells, suggesting that K11 was required for complete turnover of this substrate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated Clb5 levels in K11R mutant cells shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The turnover of all examined APC substrates is delayed in K11R mutant cells.
source: The turnover of all examined substrates is delayed in K11R mutant cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: On average, the half-lives of examined APC substrates were extended by approximately 2.5 fold in the K11R ubiquitin mutant.
source: On average, the half-lives of examined substrates were extended by approximately 2.5 fold in the K11R ubiquitin mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The half-life of Clb2 is delayed in K11R mutant cells in G1 phase.
source: The half-life of Clb2 was analyzed after addition of cycloheximide in G1 phase, revealing a delay in Clb2 turnover in K11R mutant cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hsl1 is strongly ubiquitinated in the presence of WT ubiquitin by APC-Cdh1 and Ubc4.
source: Under these conditions, Hsl1 is strongly ubiquitinated in the presence of WT ubiquitin and, to a slightly lesser extent, in reactions containing K11-only ubiquitin (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Hsl1 is ubiquitinated to a slightly lesser extent in reactions containing K11-only ubiquitin compared to WT ubiquitin.
source: Under these conditions, Hsl1 is strongly ubiquitinated in the presence of WT ubiquitin and, to a slightly lesser extent, in reactions containing K11-only ubiquitin (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The yeast APC extends monoubiquitin modifications of Hsl1 with K11-linked ubiquitin chains in vitro.
source: Significantly, the slower electrophoretic mobility of Hsl1 modified with K11-only ubiquitin relative to K0 ubiquitin shows that the yeast APC extends monoubiquitin modifications of Hsl1 with K11-linked ubiquitin chains in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophoretic mobility data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Hsl1-3K is decorated with a single monoubiquitin in reactions containing K0 ubiquitin.
source: The observation that Hsl1-3K is decorated with a single monoubiquitin in reactions containing K0 ubiquitin confirmed that a one lysine, likely K747, is ubiquitinated by the APC in Hsl1-3K (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The monoubiquitination of Hsl1-3K in the presence of K11-only ubiquitin is extended with at least two further ubiquitins, leading to a chain composed of at least three ubiquitin protomers linked through lysine-11.
source: Significantly, the monoubiquitination of Hsl1-3K in the presence of K11-only ubiquitin is extended with at least two further ubiquitins, leading to a chain composed of at least three ubiquitin protomers that are necessarily linked through lysine-11 of ubiquitin (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: K11 linkages contribute to APC-substrate turnover in yeast.
source: Altogether, our results show that K11 linkages contribute to APC-substrate turnover in yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The contribution of K11 linkages to APC-substrate turnover is appreciable only in cells without Cdc26.
source: The fact that the contribution of K11 linkages to APC-substrate turnover is appreciable only in cells without Cdc26 suggests a nuanced role of K11 linkages in yeast, similar to metazoans, wherein disruption of the gene encoding the K11-specific E2, Ube2s, is not lethal.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data and comparison to metazoan systems.

claim: K11/K48 branched chains significantly enhance substrate degradation in mammalian cells.
source: Pivotal work has shown that K11/K48 branched chains significantly enhance substrate degradation in mammalian cells (Meyer and Rape, 2014; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The yeast APC modifies substrates with a short, Ubc4-mediated heterogeneous base, in which K11-linked chains are most functionally important.
source: In light of preceding APC studies, the genetic, molecular, and biochemical results presented here suggest that the yeast APC modifies its substrates with a short, Ubc4-mediated heterogeneous base, in which K11-linked chains are most functionally important (Kirkpatrick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the study and prior literature.

claim: Ubc1 extends initial modifications with long K48-linked polyubiquitin chains in yeast APC function.
source: Ubc1 then extends those initial modifications with long K48-linked polyubiquitin chains (Rodrigo-Brenni and Morgan, 2007; Rodrigo-Brenni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In humans, K48 is part of a base chain from which homogenous K11-linked chains are extended by the APC.
source: Our data are consistent with a model whereby the human and yeast APC both use K48 and K11 linkages to attain maximal efficiency, but they do so in a reciprocal fashion; in humans, K48 is part of a base chain from which homogenous K11-linked chains are extended, whereas in yeast, K11 is the critical linkage for a base chain, from which homogenous K48 chains are extended.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the study.

claim: In yeast, K11 is the critical linkage for a base chain, from which homogenous K48 chains are extended by the APC.
source: Our data are consistent with a model whereby the human and yeast APC both use K48 and K11 linkages to attain maximal efficiency, but they do so in a reciprocal fashion; in humans, K48 is part of a base chain from which homogenous K11-linked chains are extended, whereas in yeast, K11 is the critical linkage for a base chain, from which homogenous K48 chains are extended.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The SK1 strain exhibits 92% sporulation efficiency.
source: The SK1 strain background provided a more efficient and physiologic solution, as it exhibits 92% sporulation efficiency (Deutschbauer and Davis, 2005; Ben-Ari et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The S288C strain exhibits 12% sporulation efficiency.
source: Overexpression of Ime2, a positive regulator of sporulation (Neiman, 2011), was able to increase the sporulation efficiency of S288C moderately, from 12% in wild-type diploids, to 38% (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Overexpression of Ime2 increased the sporulation efficiency of S288C from 12% to 38%.
source: Overexpression of Ime2, a positive regulator of sporulation (Neiman, 2011), was able to increase the sporulation efficiency of S288C moderately, from 12% in wild-type diploids, to 38% (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Deletion of UBI1 did not result in changes in the total ubiquitin levels or doubling time.
source: Deletion of UBI1 did not result in changes in the total ubiquitin levels or doubling time, in agreement with a previous report (Hanna et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation.

claim: Deletion of UBI2 resulted in a doubling time of 2 hr, compared to 1.6 hr for wild-type cells.
source: Deletion of UBI2 resulted in a doubling time of 2 hr, compared to 1.6 hr for wild-type cells, in agreement with a previous report (Jackson and Durocher, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation.

claim: Deletion of UBI3 resulted in a doubling time of 7 hr.
source: Deletion of UBI3 resulted in a doubling time of 7 hr, in agreement with a previous report (Jackson and Durocher, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation.
